cards.front: The sickle mutation replaces glutamate with [___] at position 6 of the β-globin chain.
cards.context:
A single base change in the β-globin gene (HBB) swaps a charged residue for a hydrophobic one.

On deoxygenation the abnormal haemoglobin polymerises into rigid fibres that deform the red cell into the classic sickle shape.

cards.front: A child with an oesophageal foreign body who is drooling and cannot swallow saliva has [___] obstruction and needs emergent endoscopy.
cards.context:
Pooling saliva means nothing is getting past — the oesophagus is completely obstructed. The child is one vomit away from aspiration, so this is an endoscopy-now problem, not a wait-and-see one.

ESGE: emergent scope preferably within 2 hours, at the latest 6.

cards.front: A 17-year-old living in a university residence has fever, confusion and a purpuric rash that has spread over an hour. The laboratory stain of her positive blood culture shows [___].
cards.context:
Fever with a fast-spreading purpuric rash in a teenager is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise. Take cultures first if possible, but never let them delay antibiotics.

Neisseria meningitidis stains pink and sits in pairs, the same look as its relative the gonococcus.

Pneumococcus forms gram-positive lancet-shaped pairs, and Haemophilus appears as small gram-negative coccobacilli.

cards.front: A 3-year-old boy was born without irises, though neither parent is affected. He has regular abdominal ultrasounds to screen for [___].
cards.context:
Sporadic aniridia can come from an 11p13 deletion that removes PAX6 and the neighbouring WT1 gene, as in WAGR syndrome. About one child in three with WAGR develops this tumour.

Renal imaging continues until genetic testing shows a PAX6 mutation alone rather than a deletion that includes WT1. Screening in high-risk syndromes runs to age 5 or 7.

The tumour grows from primitive renal blastema, usually as a well child's smooth flank mass that does not cross the midline.

cards.front: Reduced vision in a structurally normal eye, from suppressed visual input during the critical period, is [___].
cards.context:
The brain suppresses input from one eye during the critical period (strabismus, refractive error, or deprivation), so vision fails to develop even though the eye is structurally normal.

Treat early (patching/correction) — it's reversible only while the visual system is plastic.

cards.front: In a low-risk child, the only joint finding that counts as a major Jones manifestation of acute rheumatic fever is [___].
cards.context:
High-risk children also count aseptic monoarthritis or polyarthralgia as major, so a single swollen joint with a sterile aspirate can qualify.

In low-risk children polyarthralgia and aseptic monoarthritis are only minor manifestations, while in high-risk children monoarthralgia is the joint minor.

A joint finding cannot count twice: once polyarthritis is the major, arthralgia or monoarthritis cannot be added as a minor.

cards.front: ALL is the commonest childhood malignancy (~80% of paediatric leukaemias); presents with [___], thrombocytopaenia, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly; ~85-90% cured.
cards.context:
Every presenting feature traces back to blast cells crowding out normal marrow: loss of red-cell production causes anaemia (pallor, fatigue).

Loss of platelets causes thrombocytopaenia (bruising, petechiae), and marrow expansion causes bone pain.

Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy reflect leukaemic infiltration of those organs. Peak age 2-5 years; ~85-90% cured with 2-year multi-phase chemo.

cards.front: The classic EEG finding in infantile spasms (West syndrome) is [___].
cards.context:
Hypsarrhythmia is a chaotic, high-amplitude, multifocal-spike EEG pattern — the trace of a brain misfiring continuously rather than periodically.

Outcome depends on speed of recognition.

Any infant with brief, clustered spasms (especially with developmental regression) needs urgent EEG.

cards.front: Transient synovitis: sudden hip/knee pain in preschool child, often after viral URTI; child well systemically (afebrile, weight-bearing OK); resolves in [___] weeks.
cards.context:
Transient synovitis (irritable hip) is the commonest cause of hip pain in preschool children — sudden hip or referred knee pain, limp, often post-viral.

Must exclude septic arthritis (Kocher: fever >38.5, WCC >12, ESR >40, non-weight-bearing). Resolves in 1-2 weeks with rest + NSAIDs.

cards.front: Persistent childhood strabismus can impair visual development in the deviating eye, producing [___].
cards.context: The developing brain suppresses input from the misaligned eye. Early treatment aims to preserve useful vision while the visual system remains plastic.

cards.front: Gold-standard diagnosis of paediatric OSA is overnight [___]; distinguishes true OSA from primary snoring (benign).
cards.context:
PSG measures airflow, respiratory effort, oxygenation, EEG, ECG, movement to characterise sleep-disordered breathing.

Practically: overnight sleep-lab stay is expensive with long waiting lists, so many centres treat clinically without PSG when adenotonsillar hypertrophy is obvious.

cards.front: In the seriously ill child, IV access gets a maximum of [___] attempts within 90 seconds before moving to intraosseous; in arrest with no access in place, go straight to IO.
cards.context:
The taught ceiling (APLS ANZ) belongs to the seriously ill child needing urgent access — decompensated shock: a maximum of two attempts within 90 seconds, then drill.

Cardiac arrest is different: if access is not already in place, go straight to intraosseous — vein-hunting delays adrenaline that is already due.

The ceiling caps, it does not oblige: with no visible veins, IO first is always legitimate. Every resus drug and fluid runs IO at the same dose.

cards.front: A toxic, drooling child sitting forward in the tripod position with no cough suggests [___].
cards.context: The classic picture: a toxic, febrile child sitting forward (tripod), drooling, with NO barking cough — the supraglottic swelling stops the cord vibration that makes croup bark. Now rare thanks to Hib vaccination.

cards.front: The highest-risk moment for self-contamination is [___] PPE, not wearing it.
cards.context:
Most self-contamination happens on removal, not while wearing PPE — the outer surfaces are the contaminated ones and taking them off brings them past your face.

Gloves first, because they are the dirtiest thing you have; hand hygiene last, and again between steps.

cards.front: The Australian Immunisation Handbook's minimum age for a planned first DTPa-containing vaccine dose is [___].
cards.context:
The Australian Immunisation Handbook gives 6 weeks as the minimum age for a planned first DTPa-containing dose. This age is vaccine-specific, not a universal vaccine minimum.

An inadvertently early dose is assessed under separate validity rules; it is not automatically ineffective or invalid. Check the vaccine-specific table before repeating it.

cards.front: Von Willebrand disease — most common inherited bleeding disorder (~1% prevalence); vWF has two roles: platelet adhesion + carrier protein for Factor [___].
cards.context:
Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder (~1% prevalence). vWF has two roles: bridges platelets to damaged endothelium (primary haemostasis) and carries Factor VIII.

vWF deficiency thus causes mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising) AND mild factor VIII deficiency-like deep bleeding in severe types.

cards.front: In ITP the platelet count is low, but PT and APTT are [___].
cards.context:
ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia: the platelet count falls, but the coagulation cascade is intact. PT and APTT therefore remain normal.

This separates a platelet disorder from a coagulation-factor deficiency, where a clotting time becomes prolonged.

cards.front: Uncontrolled asthma = any 3-4 features (daytime symptoms, night waking, reliever use, activity limitation); partly controlled = [___] features.
cards.context:
The control framework guides stepping up therapy — escalate on the four-feature clinical assessment plus exacerbation frequency, not on FEV1 alone.

Australian thresholds: RCH defines good control as daytime and reliever use under twice weekly, night waking under twice monthly, and no activity limitation.

Some international charts count ANY night waking as loss of control; RCH and AAH both allow up to twice monthly, so use the Australian numbers here.

cards.front: Encopresis = involuntary [___] in a child over 4 years — almost always overflow incontinence from chronic constipation. Treat the constipation.
cards.context:
Encopresis (faecal soiling in a previously continent child >4 years) is almost always overflow incontinence from chronic constipation — not deliberate behaviour.

Treatment is the constipation, not the soiling.

Counsel parents that the child is not 'doing it on purpose'.

cards.front: A well 5-month-old's chest film shows a wide upper mediastinal shadow whose outer edge ripples where the anterior ribs press into it. This soft, normal structure is the [___].
cards.context:
The rippled margin is the thymic wave: the gland is soft enough for the ribs to indent it. Its right lobe can also tuck into the minor fissure to form the thymic sail.

Because it is soft, a normal thymus moulds around its neighbours and never displaces the trachea or vessels, so mass effect means something else is there.

Do not confuse it with the spinnaker sail sign, where pneumomediastinum lifts the thymus away from the heart on a cushion of air.

cards.front: An unimmunised 10-month-old has fever, irritability and a bulging fontanelle, with no rash. CSF Gram stain shows small gram-negative coccobacilli. The likely organism is [___].
cards.context:
Of the classic bacterial causes of childhood meningitis, only one looks like this on a Gram stain: small, pleomorphic forms between cocci and bacilli.

Pneumococcus shows gram-positive diplococci, and meningococcus shows gram-negative diplococci.

Type b disease, which also causes epiglottitis, is now uncommon in Australia because infants are routinely vaccinated, so a missed schedule is the clue.

cards.front: Neuroblastoma can arise anywhere along the [___] chain from neck to pelvis, but its single commonest primary site is the adrenal medulla.
cards.context:
Neural-crest cells migrate to form the paraspinal ganglia and the core of the adrenal gland, so the tumour can appear anywhere from neck to pelvis — abdomen most often, posterior mediastinum next.

An adrenal primary sits above the kidney and displaces it downward on imaging, unlike Wilms' tumour, which arises within the renal parenchyma itself.

cards.front: First-line paediatric anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 1:1000 at [___] mg/kg (capped at the adult dose) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 minutes if needed.
cards.context:
First-line for paediatric anaphylaxis is IM adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) into lateral thigh. 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) is for IM — do NOT confuse with 1:10,000 (IV cardiac arrest dose).

EpiPen Jr (0.15 mg) for 7.5-20 kg, EpiPen (0.3 mg) for >20 kg. Repeat every 5 min if needed. IM-not-IV prevents catastrophic tachyarrhythmias.

cards.front: Simple febrile convulsions carry a slightly elevated epilepsy risk of about [___]%.
cards.context:
The risk is barely above the ~1% general-population baseline because a simple febrile convulsion reflects an age-specific susceptibility to rapid temperature change, not underlying brain pathology.

So reassurance is the main treatment.

Complex febrile seizures (focal, prolonged, recurrent in 24 h) suggest a lower threshold or a structural cause, carry higher risk, and warrant work-up.

cards.front: The commonest cause of obstructive sleep apnoea in children is adenotonsillar [___].
cards.context:
Unlike adults (obesity-driven), paediatric OSA is dominated by big tonsils and adenoids, peaking 2–8 years when lymphoid tissue is largest relative to the airway.

Suspect it with snoring, witnessed pauses, and daytime behaviour problems.

cards.front: In children, Hepatitis A is [___] and never becomes a chronic carrier state, whereas Hepatitis B acquired at birth carries a high (~90%) risk of becoming chronic.
cards.context:
This is the single discriminating fact for paediatrics. Hep A is an acute illness only — the child recovers fully and never becomes a chronic carrier (no chronic-liver-disease risk).

Hep B is the opposite when caught young: the younger the child at infection, the higher the chance it becomes chronic.

A baby infected at birth has roughly a 90% chance of chronic infection (versus <5% for an infected adult) — which is the whole reason the birth-dose vaccine matters.

cards.front: Salt-wasting CAH presenting as adrenal crisis in a neonate requires IV [___] (25 mg stat) and IV 0.9% saline.
cards.context:
Salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency can cause neonatal dehydration, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and acidosis.

RCH stress-doses hydrocortisone by age: 25 mg IV/IM from birth to 2 years. Stress-dose hydrocortisone initially supplies enough mineralocorticoid activity; fludrocortisone resumes once stable.

reference.title: Adrenal crisis and acute adrenal insufficiency

cards.front: [___] methods (implants, IUDs) are recommended first-line in adolescents because efficacy is independent of daily compliance; pair with condoms for STI protection.
cards.context:
LARC (Implanon 3y, copper IUD 5-10y, Mirena 5-8y) is first-line for adolescents because efficacy is independent of daily compliance. Real-world failure <1% per year vs ~9% for daily OCPs (missed pills).

IUDs are safe in nulliparous patients — they don't affect future fertility or increase ectopic risk. Counsel adolescents about LARC explicitly; many only learn of it when an adult assumes they 'wouldn't want one'.

cards.front: Mastoiditis swelling is postero-superior to the pinna, pushing it [___] and forward; needs IV antibiotics + grommet ± cortical mastoidectomy.
cards.context:
Acute mastoiditis is the most common suppurative complication of AOM — infection spreads from middle ear into mastoid air cells.

Other features: fever, progressive ear pain despite AOM antibiotics, discharge through perforated TM, conductive hearing loss. Mostly <3y, Strep pneumoniae; CT temporal bones confirms + identifies intracranial extension.

Treat with IV 3rd-gen ceph (ceftriaxone), grommet, cortical mastoidectomy if abscess — late presentation → meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, brain abscess.

cards.front: The older collective name for the neurocutaneous syndromes, from the Greek for birthmark, is the [___].
cards.context:
The older word for this group is PHAKOMATOSES, from the Greek for a birthmark or mother-spot.

You will meet it in textbooks and in exam stems, and it means exactly the same set of conditions as 'neurocutaneous syndromes'. Worth knowing only because an unfamiliar word in a stem should not cost you the question.

cards.front: Tumour lysis syndrome metabolic derangement: high K⁺, high [___], high urate, low calcium; prevent with hydration + allopurinol/rasburicase.
cards.context:
Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is rapid cell death dumping intracellular contents into circulation, classically after starting chemo for high-tumour-burden malignancies (ALL, Burkitt's lymphoma).

Causes AKI (urate crystals + calcium phosphate deposition), cardiac arrhythmia.

Prevention: aggressive hydration + allopurinol (or rasburicase for high-risk).

cards.front: Each letter of a sickle-cell genotype is one β-globin allele (A = normal, S = sickle). Sickle cell trait, a healthy carrier, is written [___]; sickle cell disease is written HbSS.
cards.context:
HbS names the abnormal haemoglobin itself, not a genotype. A genotype needs two letters because you inherit one β-globin allele from each parent.

A is the normal allele and S is the sickle allele. So HbAS — one of each — is the healthy carrier, and HbSS is the disease.

cards.front: In abusive head trauma the subdural blood comes from tearing of the [___] veins, sheared by violent rotational acceleration–deceleration.
cards.context:
The mechanism explains the triad: violent acceleration–deceleration shears the bridging veins (which cross from cortex to the dural sinuses), producing subdural rather than extradural blood.

The same rotational forces drive the multilayered retinal haemorrhages. That the bleed is subdural and the retinal haemorrhages extend to the periphery is what separates inflicted injury from a simple fall.

cards.front: Childhood absence epilepsy: brief vacant stares in primary-school age; the clinic trigger is [___]; classic EEG is 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave.
cards.context:
Hyperventilation blows off CO₂, raising blood pH (respiratory alkalosis). This change makes absence seizures easier to trigger in susceptible children.

Animal studies suggest that alkalosis activates pH-sensitive thalamic neurons, which recruit seizure-generating circuits. The precise pathway in humans is still being worked out.

cards.front: Burns Rule of 9s: modified in children because [___] is a larger proportion (use Lund-Browder); fluid resuscitation if ≥10% TBSA (paediatric burn-fluid formula).
cards.context:
Burns assessment uses Rule of 9s, but children differ — head is a larger BSA proportion. Adult head = 9% TBSA; infant head = 18%, decreasing with age. Use the Lund-Browder chart for accuracy under 10 years.

 Fluid resuscitation is triggered at ≥10% TBSA partial-/full-thickness burns.

Current specialist paediatric guidance uses 3 mL Hartmann's × kg × %TBSA over 24 hours, plus separate maintenance fluid; give half the calculated burn-resuscitation volume in the first 8 hours from the time of injury.

cards.front: An inhaled foreign body most often lodges in the [___] main bronchus.
cards.context: The right main bronchus is wider, more vertical, and more in line with the trachea, so inhaled objects tend to go right. Suspect it after sudden choking followed by unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry.

cards.front: Generalised hypermobility becomes syndromic when paired with stretchy skin and easy bruising; this pattern suggests [___].
cards.context:
Generalised hypermobility alone is common in children.

Hyperextensible skin and easy bruising make a heritable connective-tissue disorder more likely, especially Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

cards.front: Under the RCH pathway, empiric early-onset neonatal sepsis without suspected meningitis is treated with IV [___] plus gentamicin.
cards.context:
Vertically acquired early-onset disease is dominated by GBS and E. coli; Listeria is uncommon but serious.

Under the named RCH pathway, benzylpenicillin covers GBS and Listeria while gentamicin adds Gram-negative cover when meningitis is not suspected and CSF is normal.

cards.front: In acute asthma a [___] chest on auscultation is an ominous sign of life-threatening airflow obstruction, not of improvement.
cards.context:
In acute asthma a quiet chest is dangerous, not reassuring: it means airflow is too low to generate a wheeze.

A silent chest, exhaustion, or falling SpO2 marks life-threatening asthma requiring immediate senior help and consideration of IV magnesium/salbutamol.

cards.front: In ALL, the favourable translocation is t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1, while the poor-risk t(9;22) is the [___] chromosome.
cards.context:
Two translocations carry the prognosis in paediatric ALL. t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1 is the classic GOOD-risk marker — common and chemo-sensitive. t(9;22) — the Philadelphia chromosome, BCR-ABL1.

CNS disease (leukaemic blasts in the CSF) is also adverse.

cards.front: Anaemia is first sorted by red-cell size (MCV): a low MCV is [___], and the commonest paediatric cause of that picture is iron deficiency.
cards.context:
MCV (mean corpuscular volume) is the cell-size dimension and the first branch of the work-up. Low MCV = small cells = microcytic; high = macrocytic; in-range = normocytic.

The three commonest microcytic causes are iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait, and (rarely in children) anaemia of chronic disease.

cards.front: Pertussis presents with paroxysmal cough + inspiratory 'whoop' + post-tussive vomiting; treat with azithromycin; infants <6 months may present with [___] instead.
cards.context:
Pertussis classically has three stages: catarrhal (days 1-14, URTI-like — most contagious), paroxysmal (weeks 2-6, fits with inspiratory 'whoop', post-tussive vomiting, exhaustion), convalescent (weeks 6-10).

Infants <6 months may NOT whoop — present with apnoea, cyanosis, feeding difficulty (mortality ~1 in 125).

Vaccinated individuals can still transmit — hence adult/adolescent boosters + cocoon strategy.

cards.front: The commonest cause of obstructive sleep apnoea in children is [___] hypertrophy.
cards.context:
This is why paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea is often surgical, while the adult disease is usually managed with weight loss and CPAP.

Ask about snoring, witnessed pauses and daytime behaviour — in children it presents as inattention and hyperactivity more often than sleepiness.

cards.front: A triplet repeat expansion silencing FMR1 causes [___], the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability, and boys are affected worse because the gene sits on the X.
cards.context:
A triplet-repeat expansion can silence a gene once it crosses a threshold, preventing protein production.

In fragile X, expanded FMR1 is switched off. Boys are usually more severely affected because they have no second X copy to compensate.

cards.front: The diagnostic gold standard for Hirschsprung disease is rectal suction [___] showing absent ganglion cells.
cards.context:
Hirschsprung disease: congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon (typically rectosigmoid).

Neonatal presentation: failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting. AXR shows dilated proximal bowel with absent rectal gas.

Diagnosis: contrast enema + rectal suction biopsy. Treat with primary pull-through surgery.

cards.front: Haemolysis raises the [___] bilirubin fraction, because red-cell breakdown delivers pigment to the liver faster than it can be processed.
cards.context:
Haemolysis raises bilirubin by overwhelming a normal liver with breakdown product — a problem of production, upstream of the conjugation step.

Contrast obstruction or hepatocellular disease, which traps the already-processed pigment and raises the conjugated fraction instead.

cards.front: In suspected neonatal sepsis, obtain cultures first if this causes no delay, but give antibiotics within [___] hour of the decision to treat.
cards.context:
Draw an adequate peripheral blood culture—and cultures from every central-line lumen in late-onset disease—before antibiotics when this can be done promptly.

RCH directs treatment within one hour of the decision to treat. Do not spend that hour completing every investigation in an unstable infant.

cards.front: Most common cause of paediatric gastroenteritis was [___] (now reduced by vaccination); norovirus now predominates; bacterial causes are minority.
cards.context:
Acute gastroenteritis is the commonest cause of vomiting + diarrhoea in children. Rotavirus dominated before universal vaccination; norovirus now leads.

Bacterial causes (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, ETEC) account for ~5-10%.

cards.front: Dynamic supraglottic obstruction usually produces [___] stridor; vocal-cord or subglottic obstruction is often biphasic.
cards.context:
Respiratory phase is a localisation clue, not a one-to-one map. Dynamic supraglottic obstruction such as laryngomalacia usually causes inspiratory stridor. Vocal-cord or subglottic obstruction is often biphasic.

Tracheal obstruction may be predominantly expiratory, while a fixed obstruction anywhere in the laryngotracheal airway can be biphasic.

Expiratory stridor is an upper-airway sound and should not be equated with lower-airway wheeze.

cards.front: The normal thymus in the right chest characteristically has a horizontal lower border and an outer border parallel to the chest wall — the [___].
cards.context:
On an infant chest radiograph, the normal right thymic lobe can form a triangular sail: the minor fissure creates its straight inferior border.

Gentle rib impressions create the separate thymic wave sign. Unlike a mediastinal mass, a normal thymus does not compress the airway or vessels.

cards.front: Unlike ALP, the transaminases stay close to adult values throughout childhood: an ALT above about [___] U/L is abnormal at any age.
cards.context:
The transaminases are the reassuring half of a child's LFTs: unlike ALP they sit close to adult values from infancy onwards, so an abnormal ALT means the same thing at six as at sixty.

ALT is the more liver-specific of the pair. AST also leaks from muscle, so an isolated raised AST can be rhabdomyolysis or a muscular dystrophy; a raised creatine kinase settles which.

AST runs a little higher in infancy, so a mildly raised AST with a normal ALT in a small baby is usually not liver injury.

cards.front: A non-ambulant 13-year-old boy with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy has a long C-shaped curve spanning the thoracic and lumbar spine. This curve type is [___].
cards.context:
Trunk muscles that are weak or spastic cannot support the spine, so it collapses into one long curve.

Risk rises with motor impairment, so children who cannot walk are watched closely. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy the curve typically appears once walking is lost.

That is why every curve gets a full neurological examination, looking for a cause anywhere from brain to muscle.

cards.front: An undescended testis rarely descends after [___] months of age — refer then, aiming for orchidopexy at 6-12 months.
cards.context:
Most testes that will descend do so in the first few months of life; beyond that, waiting adds nothing, so refer rather than watch.

Early surgery protects heat-sensitive germ cells — the longer a testis sits inguinal, the worse the fertility outcome. Prepubertal orchidopexy also lowers (never removes) malignancy risk and keeps the testis examinable.

cards.front: Fever for at least 5 days with conjunctivitis, rash, cervical node, strawberry tongue, and extremity changes is [___].
cards.context:
A medium-vessel vasculitis. The classic international criterion is fever for at least five days plus four of the five principal features, with no alternative diagnosis.

RCH allows the diagnosis at four days, so in Australia do not wait out a mandatory fifth day in a child who already has the features.

CRASH recalls conjunctivitis, rash, adenopathy, strawberry tongue and hand/foot changes; the features accumulate rather than appearing together.

cards.front: Under 6 months, DDH is imaged with [___]; after that, X-ray.
cards.context: The infant hip is still cartilaginous, so ultrasound is the DDH screening test until the femoral head ossifies. After about 6 months the head is visible on plain film.

cards.front: Positive skin prick test alone does NOT diagnose allergy — it shows [___]; wheal size indicates likelihood, not severity of reaction.
cards.context: Sensitisation (positive SPT or specific IgE) means the immune system has produced IgE against an allergen — but doesn't prove clinical allergy. ~10% of children are sensitised to peanut on testing.

cards.front: Air trapping is confirmed with paired [___] and expiratory chest films, or with decubitus views when the child cannot cooperate.
cards.context:
Two films confirm air trapping, and the choice between them is about whether the child can cooperate.

An older child can hold inspiration and expiration for paired frontal films. A toddler cannot, so decubitus views are used instead; brief fluoroscopy is a further option.

cards.front: Ringworm fungi obtain nutrients from keratin in skin, hair and nails. This fungal group is called [___].
cards.context:
Tinea affects keratinised tissue rather than being caused by a worm. Different sites produce different patterns, including annular skin lesions and scalp scaling with hair loss.

Scalp infection requires systemic treatment because topical therapy alone does not reach the infected hair adequately.

cards.front: Arthritis (clinical diagnosis) = joint swelling/effusion alone, OR [___]+ of tenderness, pain on movement, limited movement, increased warmth.
cards.context:
Arthritis is a clinical diagnosis. Objective joint swelling or effusion alone is enough to call it arthritis.

If there is no swelling/effusion, you need at least 2 (that is what '2+' means) of: tenderness, pain on movement, limited movement, increased warmth.

Two or more soft signs together separate true arthritis from arthralgia — joint pain with no inflammation. True arthritis triggers different workup — rheumatology referral, autoimmune screen.

cards.front: A single minor anomaly in a well baby is usually insignificant; what raises suspicion of a syndrome is finding [___] or more together.
cards.context:
Dysmorphology is pattern recognition, not face memorisation. One minor anomaly is common—about 15% of newborns have one—and is often familial.

Suspect a syndrome with at least three minor anomalies, or one alongside a major malformation, developmental delay, or growth failure. That warrants genetics referral.
